entries.text: John J. Glessner was born in Zanesville, Ohio, in 1843 and made his fortune in farm machinery as a partner in Warder, Bushnell and Glessner. In 1902 the firm joined the new International Harvester Company, where he was a vice president and chaired the executive committee.

levels.8-10: John Glessner was born in Zanesville, Ohio, in 1843. He got rich by making farm machines. He had two partners. In 1902 his company joined a big new one. It was called International Harvester. He was one of its leaders.
levels.11-13: John J. Glessner was born in Zanesville, Ohio, in 1843. He made his fortune in farm machinery as a partner in the firm of Warder, Bushnell and Glessner. In 1902 the firm joined the new International Harvester Company. There he became a vice president and led its executive committee.

entries.text: In 1885 he asked H. H. Richardson for a house, and the granite fortress at the corner of Eighteenth Street was the result: a blank face to the street and a sunny court within. The family slept here first on 1 December 1887. He lived in it until his death in 1936, a week before his ninety-third birthday.

levels.8-10: In 1885 he asked a man named H. H. Richardson to plan a house. It is made of granite, a very hard stone, and it looks like a fort. Its plain side faces the street. A sunny yard is hidden inside. The family first slept here on 1 December 1887. He lived here until he died in 1936. He was almost ninety-three.
levels.11-13: In 1885 he asked the architect H. H. Richardson to design a house. The result was this granite fortress at the corner of Eighteenth Street. It shows a plain wall to the street and hides a sunny courtyard inside. The family first slept here on 1 December 1887. He lived here until he died in 1936, a week before his ninety-third birthday.

entries.text: Frances Glessner was born Sarah Frances Macbeth in Urbana, Ohio, on New Year's Day 1848, and married John Glessner in 1870. For forty years from 1879 she kept a journal of the household, its dinners, its guests and its servants, and it is why we know this house so well.

levels.8-10: Frances Glessner was born in Urbana, Ohio, on New Year's Day 1848. Back then her name was Sarah Frances Macbeth. She married John Glessner in 1870. In 1879 she began to keep a journal about her home. She kept it for forty years. She wrote about dinners, guests and servants. That is why we know so much about this house.

entries.text: From 1893 she held her Monday Morning Reading Class in the library. She kept bees, and in 1904 she set up a silversmith's workbench in the basement and began making silver of her own.

levels.8-10: In 1893 she began a reading club. Women came to her library on Monday mornings to read. She kept bees. In 1904 she put a workbench in the basement. She began to make things out of silver.

entries.text: George Glessner was sixteen when he slept his first night in this house on 1 December 1887, and he grew up here.

levels.8-10: George Glessner was sixteen when he first slept in this house, on 1 December 1887. He grew up here.

entries.text: He married Alice Hamlin in 1898 and moved a block north to 1706, into one of the two townhouses his parents built for their children.

levels.8-10: In 1898 he married Alice Hamlin. They moved one block north, to number 1706. His parents had built two houses there for their children, and this was one of them.

entries.text: Frances Glessner was nine when the family moved in on 1 December 1887, and she grew up here. She married Blewett Lee in February 1898, and within a few years lived a block north at 1700.

levels.8-10: Frances Glessner was nine when her family moved in, on 1 December 1887. She grew up here. In 1898 she married Blewett Lee. A few years later she lived one block north, at 1700.

entries.text: As Frances Glessner Lee she later built the Nutshell Studies of Unexplained Death, tiny crime scenes for training detectives.

levels.8-10: When she grew up, her name was Frances Glessner Lee. She built tiny rooms. Each one was a crime scene. Detectives used them to learn their job. They are called the Nutshell Studies of Unexplained Death.

entries.text: Mattie Williamson was born in Inverness, Quebec, on 23 October 1859, to Irish parents. She came to the Glessners as a maid, and in February 1892 she became their cook, feeding the family and the live-in staff of eight.

levels.8-10: Mattie Williamson was born in Quebec, in Canada, on 23 October 1859. Her mom and dad came from Ireland. She first worked for the Glessners as a maid. In February 1892 she became their cook. She made the meals for the family. She fed the eight workers who lived in the house too.

entries.text: Apart from one year away, she kept the kitchen until December 1912, when she left to marry William Prescott in Los Angeles. Her brother Alex and his wife ran The Rocks, the Glessners' New Hampshire farm.

levels.8-10: She ran the kitchen until December 1912. She was away for only one year. Then she left to marry William Prescott in Los Angeles. Her brother Alex and his wife took care of The Rocks. That was the Glessners' farm in New Hampshire.

entries.text: George Glessner, the son of John and Frances Glessner, was born in 1871 and grew up in the great stone house at 1800. In 1904 he lived a block north at 1706, one of the twin townhouses his parents built for their children, with his wife Alice and a houseful of little ones.

levels.8-10: George Glessner was the son of John and Frances Glessner. He was born in 1871 and grew up in the big stone house at number 1800. In 1904 he lived one block north, at 1706. His parents had built two matching houses there for their children. He lived there with his wife, Alice, and their many small children.

entries.text: In 1915 he moved his family for good to New Hampshire, near The Rocks, the Glessners' summer estate.

levels.8-10: In 1915 he moved his family to New Hampshire to stay. They lived near The Rocks, the place where the Glessners spent their summers.

entries.text: Elizabeth Glessner, born in 1899, was about five in 1904, the eldest of George and Alice's children and a granddaughter of the house at 1800.

levels.8-10: Elizabeth Glessner was born in 1899. She was about five in 1904. She was the oldest child of George and Alice. Her grandma and grandpa lived in the big house at 1800.
levels.11-13: Elizabeth Glessner was born in 1899 and was about five in 1904. She was the eldest of George and Alice's children. Her grandparents lived in the house at 1800.
levels.14-15: Born in 1899, Elizabeth Glessner was about five years old in 1904. She was the eldest of George and Alice's children and a granddaughter of the house at 1800.

entries.text: Frances Glessner, George and Alice's second girl, was born in 1900 and named for her grandmother. Her aunt, Frances Glessner Lee, lived next door at 1700.

levels.8-10: Frances Glessner was George and Alice's second girl. She was born in 1900. She was named after her grandma. Her aunt, Frances Glessner Lee, lived next door at 1700.

entries.text: John Glessner, born in 1902, was about two in the summer of 1904, named for his grandfather in the big house down the block.

levels.8-10: John Glessner was born in 1902. He was about two years old in the summer of 1904. He was named after his grandpa, who lived in the big house down the street.

entries.text: Emily Glessner was born in 1904, the youngest of George and Alice's four children.

levels.8-10: Emily Glessner was born in 1904. She was the baby. She was the last of George and Alice's four kids.

entries.text: Frances Glessner Lee grew up in the great house at 1800 and in 1904 lived a block north at 1700, raising her children in the townhouse her parents built.

levels.8-10: Frances Glessner Lee grew up in the big house at 1800. In 1904 she lived one block north, at 1700. She raised her kids there, in a house her mom and dad built.
levels.11-13: Frances Glessner Lee grew up in the great house at 1800. In 1904 she lived a block north at 1700. She raised her children in the townhouse her parents built.

entries.text: Long after, she built the Nutshell Studies of Unexplained Death, tiny, perfect crime scenes that taught detectives to see, and came to be called the mother of forensic science.

levels.8-10: Many years later, she built tiny, perfect rooms. Each one was a crime scene. They are called the Nutshell Studies of Unexplained Death. They taught detectives how to look closely. People came to call her the mother of forensic science. That is the science of solving crimes.
levels.11-13: Many years later, she built the Nutshell Studies of Unexplained Death. These tiny, perfect crime scenes taught detectives how to see. She came to be called the mother of forensic science.

entries.text: John Glessner Lee, born in 1898, was about six in the summer of 1904, the eldest of the Lee children at 1700 and a grandson of the house at 1800.

levels.8-10: John Glessner Lee was born in 1898. He was about six in the summer of 1904. He was the oldest of the Lee children at 1700. His grandma and grandpa lived in the house at 1800.
